paragraphs.text: Anthropic's economics team has published a study called "Working with AI" that looks at how nearly 300 AI deployments are working out inside 58 US companies, according to The Decoder and AI Daily Post. The researchers conducted 66 in-person interviews at firms ranging from AI startups to established businesses in law, construction, finance, medicine and manufacturing.

Respondents said 55 percent of the deployments led to higher output or better quality work. About 19 percent, nearly one in five, had delivered no business value so far. The Decoder reported that this group breaks down into 6 percent held back by internal bottlenecks, 5 percent where time savings were eaten up by review work and 8 percent where the effect was unclear.
The sample is not representative. Every participant is an Anthropic customer, and the outcomes are self-reported by the people interviewed, both outlets noted.
The obstacles are inside the company

The most frequently mentioned obstacle, cited 49 times, was that AI produced more output than people could review. Employee resistance followed with 43 mentions and required expert reviews and testing with 42, according to The Decoder. Other problems included unstable technical infrastructure, a lack of staff to maintain tools and growing security risks. Outside factors barely came up: skeptical customers were mentioned 13 times and regulation 4 times.

The report describes uneven adoption creating friction between colleagues, with heavy users flooding coworkers with AI-written text. In one case cited by The Decoder, an employee sent the IT department seven pages of AI-generated instructions. One executive told the researchers, "A mediocre engineer with an AI is a menace to society."

Custom tools were another weak point. The Decoder reported that expensive internal AI tools often became obsolete within months or turned into rarely used apps. An accountant built an app to automate an 80-hour audit, but months later it was still not in production because a contractor had to build the final version.

Only 2 of the 58 companies reported direct layoffs tied to AI automation, and 5 had dismissed workers who refused to use AI, The Decoder reported. About two-thirds said they were hiring fewer people because of AI, and 9 firms had cut outside contractors, mostly offshore roles in software, customer support, design and legal services. Some employees described hiding their time savings from managers.

The study links larger organizational changes with higher self-reported value. It describes three approaches: giving individuals or small teams ownership of whole workflows, moving people toward work AI cannot do, such as strategy and customer relationships, and building shared, secure data infrastructure.

The findings come from a company that sells the tools in question and from interviews with its own customers, so they describe how adoption feels from the inside rather than measuring it. Even so, the pattern is consistent: the bottleneck has moved from producing work to checking it, and companies that only add AI on top of old processes report the least benefit.
The figure to watch is hiring: if two-thirds of these companies keep hiring fewer people, the effect on entry-level jobs will show up long before any wave of layoffs.
